hints.addition: Regard the two restrictions as maps on the entire copies of \(X\times\{0\}\) and \(X\times\{1\}\), not as equations at one chosen point.
Factor the proposed cylinder map through the projection \(X\times I\to X\); this proves joint continuity as well as the endpoint conditions.
Use an endpoint-exchanging continuous self-map of \(I\), and check which of \(f\) and \(g\) appears at each new endpoint.
Write the formulas on the closed halves of \(X\times I\). Besides the endpoints, check their common value on \(X\times\{1/2\}\).
Apply the pasting lemma to the two closed cylinder halves; separate continuity on each half alone does not settle agreement at their intersection.
Choose a continuous scalar coefficient that changes from \(1\) to \(0\); check the resulting vector-valued map on all of \(\mathbb R^n\times I\).
Interpolate the two values with nonnegative weights summing to one. Verify both the inequalities \(a\le H(x,t)\le b\) and continuity.
Multiply \(z\) by a unit complex number whose argument changes continuously from \(0\) to \(\pi/3\); verify the modulus throughout the deformation.
Write the cylinder map as a composite \(X\times I\to Y\to Z\). Its two restrictions should be the composites named in the question.
Use \(v\times\operatorname{id}_I:W\times I\to X\times I\) before the given homotopy; check that the time coordinate is unchanged.
Specify a single target point independent of \(x\); the terminal time slice, rather than every intermediate slice, must take that constant value.
Assume the convex target is nonempty so a contraction point can be chosen. Explain why every segment to that point stays inside the target.
Write the restriction of the cylinder map to \(A\times I\); constancy in time is stronger than agreement of only the initial and final restrictions.
Apply the fixed-subspace condition at both ends of the interval. Distinguish this necessary agreement from a sufficient criterion for constructing a relative homotopy.
For a path parameter \(s\) and deformation parameter \(t\), write separately what happens on the edges \(s=0\) and \(s=1\) of the square.
Use the relative-homotopy definition with \(A=\{x_0\}\), keeping the chosen target basepoint the same for every time slice.
A family continuous in the time variable for each fixed \(x\) need not define a continuous map on the product. Identify the missing dependence on \(x\).
Construct a piecewise-linear \(\rho\) with a plateau on \([1/3,2/3]\) and values \(0,1\) at the endpoints; compose it with the time variable of \(H\).
Use the same time parameter in both coordinates. The universal property of the product checks continuity, and the terminal pair must be independent of both input points.
Compute the scalar factor in \((1-t)x+t(-x)\). A continuous ambient formula is not a homotopy into the prescribed target when that factor vanishes.
Distinguish the map with codomain \(A\) from its composite with \(A\hookrightarrow Y\). Neither operation asserts that a homotopy in \(Y\) stays in \(A\).
Consider a contraction of an interval as a test case: its final slice collapses distinct points while the cylinder map remains continuous.
On \(\mathbb R\), interpolate between \(x\mapsto x\) and \(x\mapsto -x\). Examine the middle slice, despite both endpoint maps being homeomorphisms.
Replace one factor at a time: first hold the outer map fixed, then the inner map. Concatenate the resulting homotopies to check independence of representatives.
Check domains before writing the identities: one composite is an endomorphism of \(X\), the other of \(Y\). Equality is not required in either condition.
Check both composite conditions separately, even though this choice makes them identical strict equalities.
Exchange the domain and codomain names in the two homotopy-inverse conditions; no new deformation needs to be constructed.
Specify a terminal point in the space and a cylinder map beginning at its identity; contracting just one map into the space is not enough.
Look for a scalar multiple of \(x\) with coefficients \(1\) and \(0\) at the two times; the ambient vector-space operations give joint continuity.
The statement requires a nonempty convex set. Once \(c_0\) is chosen, use the segment from each \(x\) to \(c_0\), rather than between arbitrary pairs of points.
Only segments ending at the star center are guaranteed to lie in the set. Do not assume the stronger hypothesis of convexity.
Restrict \(r\) to the subspace with its inherited topology. A map merely taking values in \(A\) need not leave its points unchanged.
Track an element \(a\in A\) through the inclusion and back. The other composite has domain \(X\), so it expresses a different condition.
The proposed homotopy must live in \(X\); requiring its image to stay in \(A\) would generally exclude the initial identity slice.
Write an equation on \(A\times I\), not just at the two times. This is the extra relative condition beyond the chapter's deformation-retract convention.
Identify which composite is already an identity and which is supplied by the deformation. These are exactly the two homotopy-inverse tests.
Require both unit norm and agreement on already-unit vectors; also locate the excluded point where the normalization formula is undefined.
Write the coefficient as a convex combination of the positive numbers \(1\) and \(1/\|x\|\), and check the endpoint cases as well.
Substitute the unit-norm condition into the entire time-dependent coefficient, not only into the terminal retraction.
Keep the \(S^1\) coordinate unchanged, shrink the interval coordinate, and check that the bottom circle is stationary throughout.
Join a point to the contraction center, then traverse another such path backwards. Check the common value when the two paths are pasted.
Compare the degree of the identity on a circle with that of a constant map; this gives the obstruction missing from path connectedness alone.
Use the contraction to construct maps in both directions, then compare the numbers of points; a homotopy equivalence need not be bijective.
Choose \(n>0\), exhibit the contraction, and distinguish the dimension of a disk from that of the space to which it contracts.
For the return composite, write \(gvuf\) and replace \(vu\) by its homotopic identity. Treat \(ufgv\) in the other order similarly.
Parametrize the attached interval with its attachment point at \(0\). Check that linear shrinking agrees with the stationary circle at the identified endpoint.
Specify the algebraic object and the equivalence notion used to compare its values, for example isomorphism of homology groups.
Argue contrapositively: assume a homotopy equivalence and apply the invariant. The resulting forced isomorphism must contradict the computed values.
Choose positively oriented tangent bases in source and target; regularity makes the derivative an isomorphism, so its determinant has a nonzero sign.
Keep the chosen orientations and a regular value fixed. Compactness and regularity make the inverse image finite, while each summand retains its orientation sign.
Check the derivative at that unique preimage in compatible oriented charts; uniqueness of the preimage alone does not determine its sign.
The chosen value has empty inverse image and is vacuously regular. Interpret the corresponding signed sum, using the positive-dimensional hypothesis.
For oriented closed manifolds, compare the homomorphisms induced on top homology by the two maps; a homotopy makes these homomorphisms equal.
A null-homotopy identifies the induced top-dimensional homology map with that of a map factoring through a point. Use positive dimension here.
Track a chosen fundamental class through \(f_*\) and then \(g_*\); the two integer multipliers occur successively, not additively.
Introduce a homotopy inverse and take the degree of its composite with \(f\). Ask which pairs of integers have product \(1\).
Use \(1\in S^1\) as a regular value and count its seventh roots; check the direction of the angle map near each root.
Write the map in angle coordinates and track the sign of the angular derivative, rather than counting four preimages without signs.
Separate necessity, from homotopy invariance, from sufficiency, which uses the classification theorem specifically for circle maps.
Extend the reflection to an ambient linear map with one negative eigenvalue, and compare its determinant with the induced boundary orientation sign.
Distinguish the circle's dimension from that of its ambient plane when substituting in the antipodal formula.
Count sign reversals in the three-dimensional ambient space. Reversing all ambient coordinates is not the same as reversing two tangent coordinates in isolation.
The relevant determinant is that of \(-I\) on \(\mathbb R^4\). Determine the parity of its number of negative eigenvalues.
Apply multiplicativity before doing the integer arithmetic, and keep the order of the named composite clear.
Assume a homotopy inverse exists and derive an equation \(2k=1\) for an integer \(k\); this exposes the obstruction directly.
In the smooth case, a missed point is a regular value with empty fiber. For a continuous sphere map, factor through the contractible punctured sphere instead.
Compare the change in unsigned count with the contribution \((+1)+(-1)\) of a newly created pair; only one of these quantities cancels.
Apply degree to the strict retraction equation on \(S^n\), with the same orientation used for both copies of the sphere.
Contract the inclusion inside the disk first, then postcompose the entire homotopy by the hypothetical retraction; the intermediate maps need not land on the boundary before postcomposition.
Compute the degree of the same composite in two ways: from its identity property and from its factorization through a contractible space.
Try a circle map \(e^{it}\mapsto e^{i(t+2\sin t)}\). Its angle increases by \(2\pi\) over one period, but its derivative changes sign.
Compare the parity-dependent degree of antipodes with the identity degree; this specifies a concrete obstruction to test in VIII/04 rather than just a chapter reference.
Compute the two successive ambient sign changes, and check that both intermediate and final vectors still lie on the unit sphere.
Solve the fixed-point equation in the ambient real vector space, then impose the sphere's unit-norm condition.
Use the determinant of \(-I\) in \(\mathbb R^5\); the exponent counts ambient coordinates, not the sphere dimension alone.
There are six ambient coordinate sign reversals for \(S^5\). Relate their parity to the orientation sign.
Use homotopy invariance to obtain a necessary equality of degrees. Equality by itself is not being used here as a general classification theorem.
Specify that the assertion concerns every continuous map and at least one pair \(x,-x\), with equality in both real coordinates simultaneously.
Equal antipodal images combined with oddness would force the common image to be zero; test whether zero belongs to the unit-sphere target.
First prove the denominator is nowhere zero from antipode separation. Then check continuity and that the normalized vector has unit norm.
Compute the numerator and its norm separately after replacing \(x\) by \(-x\); the norm is unchanged by sign reversal.
Set \(h(x)=f(x)-f(-x)\) and restrict to a semicircle joining antipodes. Its endpoint values allow an intermediate-value argument.
Describe both the equivalence relation and the quotient topology; naming the orbit set alone does not specify the topological space.
Intersect a line through the origin with \(S^n\); determine the pair of unit representatives and compare it with one antipodal equivalence class.
Define a candidate map on classes by \([x]\mapsto f(x)\). Separate well-definedness on each two-point fiber from continuity supplied by the quotient property.
Compare the two points of \(S^0\) with their single orbit under the antipodal involution.
Represent a line by an angle modulo \(\pi\) and double the angle to obtain a well-defined point on the circle.
Seek a circle map unchanged when \(z\) is replaced by \(-z\); then check that its fibers contain exactly those two points.
Use the angle-doubling identification from the preceding exercise with its chosen orientation; an arbitrary orientation change of the target changes the degree's sign.
After stereographic projection, verify that neighborhoods of the omitted pole correspond to complements of compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
Use height \(t\in[-1,1]\) and the map \((x,t)\mapsto(\sqrt{1-t^2}x,t)\); examine what happens at the two extreme heights.
Count the dimensions in the filtration \(\mathbb RP^0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb RP^n\), remembering the zero-dimensional cell.
With the last coordinate fixed to zero, the remaining coordinates still satisfy one unit-sphere equation in \(\mathbb R^n\).
On the upper hemisphere recover the last coordinate as \(\sqrt{1-\|u\|^2}\). This constructs the inverse to projection, including the boundary.
A contraction would make the identity homotopic to a constant sphere map. Compare their degrees, keeping the condition \(n\ge1\).
Normalize projective coordinates with nonzero last coordinate to \(1\). Identify this open \(\mathbb R^n\) chart as the new cell and the complementary projective subspace as the old skeleton.
Identify only boundary points with their prescribed images; explain which equivalence classes contain points of the disk interior.
For \(n>0\), compare the dimensions of the disk, its interior, and its boundary; treat the zero-cell boundary as empty.
Start with the quotient map on \(X\sqcup D^n\), then restrict its domain to the new disk, including its boundary.
Check that no interior point is identified with another point; do not extend this injectivity claim to the disk boundary.
A point \(u\) on the boundary represents both a disk point and \(\varphi(u)\) in the old space; their proposed images must agree.
Since there are no boundary points to identify, use the disjoint-union topology to decide how the new point meets \(X\).
The two endpoint images may coincide or differ; compare the loop-forming and edge-joining possibilities.
Parametrize the interval by \(t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}\), and check precisely which endpoint identification makes this descend.
Assign each edge an interval and record its two endpoint vertices; loops and multiple edges are allowed in this CW description.
Use a disk as a compactification of its interior after collapsing the boundary; check that the collapsed class is the single point at infinity.
The entire boundary is identified to the chosen basepoint, while the disk interior stays separate from the old space.
Write \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and let the output angle advance by \(m\theta\); negative integers must reverse winding direction.
The old circle is identified with the new disk's actual boundary, not collapsed to a point as in the sphere construction.
Keep the old circle and replace the disk with its boundary quotient; identify the single point where these two pieces meet.
In the disk model of \(\mathbb RP^2\), opposite boundary points represent the same line; track the boundary map after identifying \(\mathbb RP^1\) with a circle.
For \(n>0\), collapse the boundary of one \(n\)-disk to the old vertex; for \(n=0\), regard \(S^0\) as two vertices.
Track the equivalence classes of the square's four vertices and its pairs of opposite edges before counting the open interior.
Choose orientations on the two identified edges and read the oriented square boundary once, using inverses when traversal opposes the chosen edge direction.
Use a \(4g\)-gon with paired sides; count the resulting vertex class, distinct edge pairs, and open polygon interior.
Group the oriented boundary traversal into one four-letter block for each handle, retaining the order of the blocks.
The projective chart with last homogeneous coordinate nonzero is an open \(n\)-cell; its complement is the old projective subspace.
Check that the boundary of every included cell lands in a lower skeleton, so the stopped construction is closed under attachments.
Use a radial parameter to identify the cone on the attaching sphere with a disk, with cone base corresponding to disk boundary.
Compare the constant and identity attachments of a two-cell to a circle: the cell dimensions agree, but one retains a circle homotopy class and the other fills it.
Separate the finiteness assertion about each closed cell from the topological test using characteristic maps of all closed disks.
Include every dimension \(0\) through \(n\), not merely the cells of exactly dimension \(n\).
Identify the starting object before any zero-cells have been attached; no points have yet been introduced.
Write one attaching map \(S^{n-1}_\alpha\to X^{n-1}\) per new cell and form the pushout of the disjoint union of boundary inclusions.
An infinite number of cells need not imply unbounded dimension; compare an infinite graph with projective space of unbounded dimension.
Apply the weak-topology test to an arbitrary subset: its inverse image in each characteristic zero-disk is automatically open and closed.
Record each one-cell's two endpoints and allow them to coincide; this captures loops as well as ordinary edges.
Distinguish finitely many cells in total from finitely many cells in each dimension and from finite dimension.
Map the finite disjoint union of closed characteristic disks onto the complex; use compactness of that union and continuity of the quotient map.
Including an open cell obliges you to include all boundary cells in its closure, rather than only selected interior points.
The attaching boundary of a cell of dimension at most \(n\) lies in a lower skeleton, so check the subcomplex condition cell by cell.
The requirement concerns every skeleton simultaneously; it does not require individual cells to map bijectively to cells.
Use \(D^n/\partial D^n\) for \(n>0\); check separately that \(S^0\) has two zero-cells.
In the square quotient, count vertex equivalence classes and edge equivalence classes before the single open face.
At each inclusion \(\mathbb RP^{k-1}\subset\mathbb RP^k\), identify the complement as \(\mathbb R^k\).
Subdivide a circle edge by adding a vertex; compare its old and new vertex and edge counts without changing the underlying space.
State the quantifiers in the order: for each point, there exists a neighborhood, meeting only finitely many cells.
Use an infinite wedge of circles: each individual closed edge meets finitely many cells, while every neighborhood of the wedge point meets infinitely many edges.
Test the composite on each closed characteristic disk, including its boundary; continuity on open cells alone is insufficient.
After identifying finitely many cells met by the compact set, use closure finiteness to place them inside a finite subcomplex.
The subspace must be a union of whole cells together with their boundary cells, not an arbitrary subset of a CW complex.
For nonempty \(A\), first record the new collapsed vertex, then inspect the characteristic maps of cells outside \(A\).
Use the alternating cell count with dimensions attached to each number; this prevents adding both edge contributions with the wrong sign.
The top cell contributes according to the parity of \(n\); distinguish the even- and odd-dimensional cases, including \(S^0\).
Specify which end becomes the vertex and which end remains the cone base; this convention determines the later attaching identifications.
For a representative \([a,s]\), vary the height toward \(1\) and verify that representatives of the existing vertex always have the same image.
Collapse each end separately, obtaining two suspension points; identifying both ends to the same point would be a different quotient.
Use latitude as suspension height and shrink the \(S^n\) factor to a point at each of the two poles.
Write the boundary relation \((a,0)\sim f(a)\) as well as the common cone-vertex relation at height \(1\).
Identify the cone base with the boundary of the new disk, keeping the original map into \(X\) as the attaching map.
The copy of \(A\) in the target is already the cone base after gluing by the identity; no additional boundary collapse occurs.
Collapsing the cone base to the target point creates the second suspension pole, distinct from the existing cone vertex.
Retain the CW-subcomplex hypothesis and use the cofiber-to-quotient comparison; its conclusion is a homotopy equivalence, not an automatic homeomorphism.
The second arrow includes the old target space into the cone attachment; check its composite with \(f\) contracts along the cone direction.
Collapse the entire copy of \(X\) in \(C_f\); the cone base and cone vertex then become the two suspension poles.
Gluing the disk boundary bijectively to the existing circle simply makes that circle the boundary of the filled disk.
Track the degree-two boundary identification in the disk model of the projective plane, rather than treating the cone as a suspension.
The constant attachment collapses only the new disk's boundary to one point of the old circle; identify the resulting sphere summand.
For \(m\ne0\), the two relevant cellular groups are linked by multiplication by \(m\); locate the cokernel degree and the kernel degree separately.
Identify the base end using \(f\) but leave all free-end points distinct; this is precisely the distinction from \(C_f\).
The collapsed subspace is the free copy of the domain, not the old target \(X\); those two collapses yield different constructions.
Decrease the cylinder height to zero and keep every point of \(X\) fixed; check agreement at each glued point \((a,0)\).
On a cone representative use \([a,t]\mapsto[u(a),t]\); on \(X\) use \(v\). Commutativity checks their agreement on the glued base.
Choose a null-homotopy to replace \(f\) by a constant map, then identify the attached cone with a suspension joined at its basepoint.
A homotopy changes attaching data through continuous deformations; the comparison provides homotopy inverses, not generally a pointwise bijection of quotients.
List the relations at heights \(0\) and \(1\) separately, and check that no extra identifications are imposed at interior heights.
For a CW pair, combine the cone-to-quotient equivalence with the interpretation of reduced homology of \(X/A\) as relative homology.
Locate the sphere-boundary inclusion that permits homotopy extension; it controls how a deformation of attaching data changes the whole attachment.
The prescribed maps must agree on \(A\times\{0\}\); ask for an extension from \((X\times\{0\})\cup(A\times I)\) to the full cylinder.
Include the quantifier over all target spaces and all compatible initial maps and subspace homotopies for the specified inclusion.
Check that the subspace consists of cells together with their attaching boundaries, so the standard CW-pair homotopy-extension theorem applies.
State the common source, common target, and homotopy between the two attaching maps before identifying the two adjunction spaces to compare.
Ask whether the construction supplies a continuous bijection or maps inverse only up to homotopy; the theorem guarantees only the latter.
Use the two ends of \(S^{n-1}\times I\) for the two boundary maps; the side carries their joint continuous interpolation.
Replace \(\varphi\) by its constant representative and identify \(D^n/\partial D^n\), while retaining the old space \(X\).
Use the classification theorem for circle maps, not just the fact that degree is invariant; sufficiency is special information.
First convert equal degrees into a homotopy of circle maps, then invoke homotopy invariance of the cell attachment.
Form the disjoint union of the homotopies on the separate boundary spheres; check the associated CW pushout rather than assuming arbitrary quotients behave well.
For the selected boundary subspace \(B\), require \(H(b,t)\) to be independent of \(t\); endpoint agreement alone is not a relative homotopy.
Use the cone-cylinder model to replace a sphere domain by \(A\), and retain the hypotheses supporting the homotopy pushout comparison.
Identify the extension problem on the old space and attaching collar; HEP supplies the compatible ambient deformation missing from a set-theoretic quotient argument.
Do not transfer local point-set properties merely from homotopy equivalence; the comparison theorem does not claim the quotients have the same local neighborhoods.
Keep the target \(X\) and cell dimension fixed when replacing the attaching map by a representative of its homotopy class.
The new disk has dimension two while its boundary loop has dimension one; keep this shift when identifying the wedge summand.
Use the collar carrying \(H\) to compare the endpoint attachments, then identify the retractions or comparison maps proving the endpoint homotopy types agree.
A reparameterization or deformation may alter every pointwise formula while keeping its class in \([S^{n-1},X]\) unchanged.
Distinguish a fixed pair's HEP from a claim about all subsets, and include compatibility with the chosen initial map.
Choose a CW structure on the disk containing its boundary as a subcomplex; apply the corresponding subcomplex-cofibration result.
Separate exact quotient data from homotopy-type data: raw attaching formulas specify the quotient, whereas homotopy classes suffice for the theorem's weaker conclusion.
Replace an attached disk by the cone on its boundary; this identifies the attachment comparison as a particular mapping-cone comparison.
Choose a basepoint and a path to the attaching loop when necessary; free loop classes correspond to conjugacy classes rather than a canonical based element.
At one skeleton, replace a complicated boundary map by a homotopic representative with simpler combinatorics; check the CW hypotheses before proceeding to later attachments.
Specify both endpoint equations and the target space; continuity is required on the whole closed interval.
The two equal endpoint values must be the designated basepoint, not an unspecified point of the space.
Check how the endpoint values change under \(t\mapsto1-t\), and apply the operation twice as a consistency test.
Evaluate the proposed two pieces at the joining time; mismatched endpoints prevent the pasting lemma from applying.
Rescale each half-interval to \(I\), retaining this chapter's convention that \(\alpha\) is traversed before \(\beta\).
Use a square with path coordinate \(s\) and homotopy coordinate \(t\); the two vertical edges must remain at the fixed endpoints.
Distinguish individual loops from their relative-homotopy classes, then define multiplication on those classes by representative concatenation.
A constant segment changes the timing of a concatenated loop; use endpoint-preserving reparameterization to verify the identity law on classes.
Contract the path followed by its reverse by shortening the distance traveled along it, keeping the basepoint fixed throughout.
Paste the two path homotopies along the rescaled path coordinate; their stationary common endpoint ensures continuity on the joining edge.
Locate the three traversal intervals in each parenthesization; a piecewise-linear change of timing compares them relative to the endpoints.
Path connectedness is part of the definition; trivial groups in separate components alone do not make their disjoint union simply connected.
Use two enlarged hemispheres and van Kampen: their intersection is path connected for \(n\ge2\), while each hemisphere neighborhood is contractible.
Lift a loop to \(\mathbb R\) through \(t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}\) with fixed starting point; inspect its integer endpoint displacement.
Use the lift \(t\mapsto nt\) starting at zero and distinguish positive from negative displacement.
Apply the circle map to the positively oriented generator; its induced homomorphism on \(\mathbb Z\) multiplies by the degree.
Postcompose both a loop and any endpoint-fixing homotopy with \(f\); this proves the assignment is independent of the representative.
Evaluate both proposed homomorphisms on an arbitrary loop class, following the order of the two map compositions.
For a loop \(\alpha\), substitute \(\alpha(s)\) into the given based homotopy; the resulting square keeps both path endpoints fixed.
Track the path traced by the basepoint under a nonbased homotopy; the induced isomorphism requires that basepoint change, not an unsupported equality of based maps.
The inverse to projection pairs two loops with the same time parameter; pair their homotopies to check well-definedness.
Choose generators by traversing each circle coordinate with the other fixed; use the product formula, not the free-group formula for a wedge.
The attached disk supplies a null-homotopy of its boundary loop; at the group level the relation is imposed through its normal closure.
Fix the initial lift of a circle loop and compare its endpoints under \(\mathbb R\to S^1\); this motivates the general path-lifting theorem.
Require the sheets to be open and pairwise disjoint, and check that each restriction maps onto the same entire neighborhood \(U\).
A local inverse near one point upstairs is not enough: one neighborhood downstairs must simultaneously account for its whole preimage.
Distinguish the fiber \(p^{-1}(x)\) from the preimage of a neighborhood, which is a union of open sheets.
Intersect one open sheet with \(p^{-1}(x)\); the homeomorphism onto an evenly covered neighborhood makes this intersection a singleton.
Count points over a fixed basepoint, not connected components of the total space; a connected cover can have several sheets.
An evenly covered neighborhood identifies its fibers with the same sheet-index set. Thus fiber cardinality is locally constant before connectedness is used.
Choose an arc shorter than a full turn and lift its angle to disjoint intervals differing by integers; also check that the total space is simply connected.
Divide the angle by \(2\pi\) and use the periodicity of the complex exponential to identify every solution, including negative ones.
For \(n\ge1\), solve \(z^n=w\) on a small arc and separate its \(n\) continuous root branches.
The discreteness of \(F\) makes every \(X\times\{a\}\) an open sheet mapping homeomorphically onto \(X\).
Restrict \(p\) to the unique sheet containing a chosen point upstairs; that restriction supplies the required local homeomorphism.
Test the projection \(\mathbb R\sqcup(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) given by inclusion on each summand: compare fiber cardinalities near zero.
Intersect an evenly covered neighborhood with \(A\) and its sheets with \(p^{-1}(A)\); use the subspace topologies on both sides.
Form a subspace of \(Y\times\widetilde X\), not an unrestricted product: both coordinates must represent the same point of \(X\).
Over \(f^{-1}(U)\), each sheet of \(p\) supplies a graph \(y\mapsto(y,s(f(y)))\); use these graphs to verify the local covering model.
Include path connectedness in simple connectivity and keep the covering condition separate from the condition on its total space.
Check both ingredients: the antipodal quotient is a double cover, and \(S^n\) is simply connected in the stated range \(n\ge2\).
Type the maps carefully: \(s:X\to\widetilde X\), so the right-inverse equation is an equality of maps from \(X\) to itself.
Choose a sheet \(V\) above \(U\); the inverse of \(p|_V\) is continuous and its composite with \(p\) is \(\operatorname{id}_U\).
The commuting equation holds over the fixed base, and \(h\) must be a homeomorphism, not merely a bijection between fibers.
Start with an upstairs loop whose projection is null-homotopic; lift the based null-homotopy to show the original upstairs class vanishes.
Compute the image of the upstairs fundamental group under \(p_*\); simple connectivity makes the source group trivial.
Identify the fiber with cosets of the covering subgroup after choosing a basepoint and a left/right action convention; count those cosets.
For a path downstairs, specify one starting point upstairs, then ask separately whether a lift exists, is unique, and returns to its starting fiber point.
Check the types \(\widetilde f:Y\to\widetilde X\) and \(p:\widetilde X\to X\); their composite must equal the given map on all of \(Y\).
The chosen point must lie over \(\alpha(0)\). Different choices in that fiber generally produce different lifts of the same path.
Inside an evenly covered neighborhood, the starting sheet forces the local inverse; propagate this agreement along the interval.
Use compactness of \(I\) to choose a finite subdivision subordinate to evenly covered neighborhoods, then match adjacent lifted endpoints.
Show that both the agreement set and its complement are open using local sheets; connectedness and one agreement point finish the argument.
Prescribe a continuous lift of the entire initial map \(H(-,0)\), not just one initial point when the parameter space is an arbitrary \(Y\).
The lifted endpoint varies continuously with the homotopy parameter inside a discrete fiber. A continuous path in that fiber must be constant.
For one direction project the closed lift; for the other lift a representative of an upstairs loop and use invariance of lifted endpoints.
Lift a based null-homotopy of the projected loop, keeping its boundary in the appropriate fiber; compare the resulting lift with the original loop.
Choose compatible basepoints and assume the usual path-connected, locally path-connected domain. Compare images inside the same based group \(\pi_1(X,x_0)\).
For each \(y\), lift \(f\circ\gamma\) from the chosen point over \(f(y_0)\); the next task is to prove its endpoint is independent of \(\gamma\).
Join one candidate path to the reverse of the other. The subgroup hypothesis forces the image loop to have a closed lift.
Apply \(p_*\) to the trivial group of the simply connected total space; do not identify this subgroup with all of \(\pi_1(X)\).
Substitute the trivial covering subgroup into the based lifting criterion, retaining its local hypotheses on the domain.
Every homomorphism from \(\pi_1(Y)=0\) has trivial image, which lies in any covering subgroup; choose the lifted basepoint before applying the criterion.
With \(p(t)=e^{2\pi it}\), the equation is \(e^{2\pi i\widetilde f(y)}=f(y)\); the usual angle in radians is \(2\pi\widetilde f\).
Write the desired equation \(g(y)^n=f(y)\) and view \(g\) as a map to the total circle of the power covering.
The induced image of the degree-\(m\) map is \(m\mathbb Z\); determine when this subgroup lies in the image \(n\mathbb Z\) of the covering map.
Lift each loop from each point of the fiber and retain its endpoint; state the concatenation convention before deciding whether this is a left or right action.
Apply homotopy lifting to an endpoint-fixed loop homotopy; the lifted boundary tracks lie in discrete fibers and cannot move.
Local path connectedness makes a connected covering space path connected. Project a path joining two points of the same fiber to obtain the required loop downstairs.
Keep the chosen point \(\tilde x_0\) in the notation: changing it can change the subgroup by conjugation rather than equality.
Compare the subgroup definition with the closed-lift criterion in both directions, always lifting from the designated \(\tilde x_0\).
Type the self-lift correctly: a deck map \(h:\widetilde X\to\widetilde X\) satisfies \(p\circ h=p\). It lifts \(p\) through itself; a lift of \(\operatorname{id}_X\) would instead be a section.
The map acts on the total space and obeys \(p\circ h=p\); distinguish this from a section, whose domain is the base.
Evaluate the commuting equation at an arbitrary \(\tilde x\in p^{-1}(x)\), then identify the fiber containing \(h(\tilde x)\).
Check that the identity, composition, and inverse of homeomorphisms satisfying \(ph=p\) again satisfy that same equation.
Two deck maps are lifts of the same map \(p\); apply uniqueness for lifts on a connected domain when their values agree once.
Compare the given map with \(\operatorname{id}_{\widetilde X}\) as two lifts of \(p\), using the fixed point as their common value.
